blocks.prompt: The Tadpole That Ate Its Own Tail
blocks.text: A frog does not start out as a frog. It starts as an egg, one of hundreds in a clump of clear jelly floating in a pond. Inside each egg, a tiny black dot grows. Soon a tadpole wiggles free. A tadpole has no legs at all. It has a long tail for swimming and gills for breathing under the water. It spends its days scraping green algae off rocks. Then its body starts to change. Back legs push out first. Front legs come next. The tail shrinks away, and the tadpole is a frog.

blocks.prompt: From Jelly to Frog
blocks.text: In early spring, a frog lays her eggs in a pond. Not one egg or two, but hundreds, wrapped together in a blob of clear jelly. The jelly swells up with water. It holds the eggs together and keeps them a little warmer than the pond around them. After two or three weeks, tadpoles wriggle out. A tadpole looks nothing like its mother. It has no legs, no lungs, and no eyelids. It has a long flat tail and gills, and it breathes underwater the way a fish does. All day it scrapes algae off stones with rows of tiny hard ridges around its mouth. Then the changing starts. Two back legs push out near the tail. Lungs begin to grow inside, so the tadpole swims up to gulp air. Front legs are growing too, but hidden under the skin, and one day they simply pop through. Last of all, the tail gets shorter and shorter. It does not fall off. The frog's body takes it apart and uses it as food while the young frog is too busy changing to eat.

blocks.prompt: Double Life
blocks.text: Amphibian is a Greek word. It means double life, and no animal earns the name better than a frog. The first life begins as an egg. A female frog lays her eggs in water, sometimes hundreds at once, bound together in clear jelly that swells and protects them. Inside, a dark speck slowly organizes itself into an animal. In a few weeks the tadpole breaks out. A tadpole is built for a completely different world than the frog it will become. It has gills instead of lungs, a long muscular tail instead of legs, and a mouth ringed with tiny hard ridges for scraping algae off rocks. Its intestine is long and tightly coiled, because plant food is hard to digest and has to be worked on for a long time. Then a gland in the tadpole's throat releases thyroid hormone, and the whole body begins to rebuild itself. Hind legs bud out first. Lungs form, so the tadpole starts rising to the surface for air. Front legs develop under a flap of skin and burst through later. The eyes shift upward and bulge out. The long plant-eating gut shortens into a short hunter's gut, because the frog will eat insects, not algae. Last, the tail vanishes. It is not shed. The body dismantles it cell by cell and recycles the material, which is useful, because a frog in the middle of metamorphosis cannot eat. What climbs out of the pond is the same animal, rebuilt from the inside out.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: The word amphibian comes from Greek and means double life. It is not a poetic exaggeration. A frog really does live two lives, in two different bodies, and it builds the second one out of the first. Life one begins in water. A female frog releases her eggs, often several hundred at a time, and they clump together inside a mass of clear jelly. The jelly absorbs water and swells, cushioning the eggs and holding a little warmth. Inside each capsule a dark speck divides and folds and organizes itself, and within two or three weeks a tadpole wriggles free. A tadpole is not a small frog. It is a different design entirely, suited to a different job. It breathes through gills. It swims with a long muscular tail and has no limbs at all. Around its mouth sit rows of tiny keratin ridges, sometimes called labial teeth, which it uses to rasp algae off stones. Because plant matter is difficult to break down, its intestine is unusually long and tightly coiled, packed into its round body like rope in a bucket. Then a chemical signal changes everything. The tadpole's thyroid gland floods its blood with hormone, and metamorphosis begins. Hind limbs bud out beside the tail. Lungs develop, and the tadpole starts rising to gulp air. Forelimbs grow hidden beneath a flap of skin and break through later, which is why a frog appears to sprout back legs first. The eyes migrate upward and gain lids. The long grazing gut shortens dramatically, because the adult will hunt insects, not scrape at stones. Finally the tail disappears. It is not dropped or bitten off. The frog's own cells take it apart piece by piece and reuse the material, which matters, because a young frog in the middle of metamorphosis cannot eat. The schedule is not fixed. A common frog might finish in about three months. An American bullfrog in a cold northern pond can spend two years as a tadpole. Some spadefoot toads, hatching into desert puddles that will be gone in days, race through the whole transformation in about two weeks. And a few frogs skip the pond altogether. The coqui of Puerto Rico lays its eggs on damp land, and what hatches is not a tadpole but a frog the size of a pea.

blocks.prompt: Two Animals, One Name
blocks.text: Every frog is two animals with one name. This is not a figure of speech. The animal that hatches in the pond and the animal that hops out of it are built to different plans, eat different food, breathe by different means, and move by different machinery. Somewhere in between, one is taken apart and the other is assembled from the pieces. Biologists call it metamorphosis, and the word does not do it justice. Start with the egg. A female frog releases her clutch into water, sometimes several hundred at once, and a coat of jelly around each egg swells as it takes on water. The jelly is not decoration. It cushions the embryo, holds a small amount of warmth, and makes the whole mass awkward for a small mouth to swallow. Inside, a dark speck divides, folds, and organizes itself into something with a head and a tail. What emerges is not a small frog. It is a tadpole, and a tadpole is a finished animal, not a rough draft. It breathes with gills. It swims with a muscular tail and has no limbs at all. Around its mouth are rows of hard keratin ridges that work like a rasp, scraping algae from stones. Plant food is stubborn and slow to digest, so the tadpole carries an intestine that is enormously long and coiled tight inside its round body. Every part of it is solving the problem of being a small grazing animal in still water. None of it is useful to a frog. Then the tadpole's thyroid gland releases a surge of hormone, and the rebuilding begins. Hind limbs bud out beside the tail. Lungs form, and the tadpole starts breaking the surface to gulp air. Forelimbs are already growing, but hidden beneath a flap of skin, which is why a frog seems to sprout its back legs first and its front legs overnight. The eyes climb toward the top of the skull and acquire lids. The mouth widens into the trap of a predator. The long grazing gut shortens drastically, because the adult will swallow insects whole rather than graze. And the tail, that superb swimming organ, is not shed and not bitten off. The frog's own cells dismantle it, molecule by molecule, and carry the material away to build the animal that is replacing it. This is fortunate, because a frog in the middle of metamorphosis has a mouth and a gut that suit neither diet, and it cannot eat at all. The tail is its lunch. The timetable is nothing like fixed. A common frog may finish in about three months. An American bullfrog in a cold pond can remain a tadpole for two years or more, growing large and waiting. Spadefoot toads, which breed in desert pools that vanish within weeks of the rain that made them, can sprint through the entire transformation in roughly two weeks. Same process, wildly different clocks, because the pond sets the deadline. Some frogs decline the whole arrangement. The coqui of Puerto Rico lays its eggs on damp leaves, and what hatches is not a tadpole but a frog small enough to sit on a fingernail, the tadpole stage compressed and completed inside the egg. The male Surinam toad presses fertilized eggs into the skin of the female's back, where they sink in, seal over, and later push out as fully formed toadlets. Darwin's frog is stranger yet: the male takes the tadpoles into his vocal sac and carries them until they are frogs. The lesson worth taking from a pond is this. There is no single frog life cycle, only a set of solutions to one problem: how do you get an egg laid in water to become an animal that lives out of it. Most frogs solve it with a tadpole. A few solve it by skipping the tadpole and paying for the shortcut in yolk and parental effort. Evolution is not tidy. It is a long argument between an animal and the place it lives, and the frog is one of the answers.
